course.title: Unity C# Scripting & Engine Architecture: Professional Patterns, Systems & Engine Programming
course.description: Parts 1-5 of 20: Advanced DI with Zenject, Command Pattern with undo/redo, Reactive Programming with UniRx, ECS deep dive with baking, and DOTS Physics with deterministic simulation.

blocks.value: Beyond Manual DI: Zenject (Extenject)

Manual DI containers work for small projects, but production games need automatic binding, scene injection, sub-containers, and lifecycle management. Zenject (now Extenject, the community fork) is the industry-standard DI framework for Unity.

items: Automatic binding via attributes: [Inject], [InjectOptional], [Inject(Id = "Player")]
Scene installers wire dependencies without code changes
Sub-containers isolate systems (e.g., each level has its own container)
Factory bindings with runtime parameters
Memory pools integrated with DI for zero-allocation spawning

blocks.output: Zenject installer with singleton bindings, factory with memory pool, method injection with ID-qualified parameters, and IPoolable lifecycle.

blocks.value: Sub-Containers & Scene Contexts

blocks.output: Project-level vs scene-level installers, sub-containers for isolated systems, and decorator pattern for cross-cutting concerns.

blocks.question: What is the main advantage of using Zenject/Extenject over a manual DI container?
options: Zenject runs faster at runtime
Zenject provides automatic binding, memory pools, sub-containers, and scene injection out of the box
Zenject requires less code to set up
Zenject is officially supported by Unity
blocks.correctAnswer: Zenject provides automatic binding, memory pools, sub-containers, and scene injection out of the box
blocks.explanation: While a manual DI container teaches the fundamentals, Zenject adds production features: automatic [Inject] resolution, integrated memory pools (IPoolable), sub-containers for isolation, decorator bindings, and scene context installers. These are essential for large teams and complex projects but would take months to build manually.

parts.partTitle: Part 2: Command Pattern, Undo/Redo & Action History

blocks.value: Command Pattern for Reversible Operations

The Command Pattern encapsulates operations as objects, enabling undo/redo, action queuing, and macro recording. Essential for level editors, turn-based games, and any system requiring reversible state changes.

blocks.output: ICommand interface with Execute/Undo and three concrete commands: MoveEntity, DamageEntity, and SpawnEntity with full state capture.

blocks.value: Command History Manager

blocks.output: CommandHistory with branching undo/redo, max size trimming, events, and MacroCommand for composite operations. Level editor controller demonstrates spawn + undo/redo hotkeys.

blocks.question: Why is the Command Pattern superior to directly modifying state for operations that need undo support?
options: Commands run faster than direct state changes
Commands encapsulate both the operation and its reversal logic, making undo/redo trivial
Commands use less memory
Commands are required by Unity's API
blocks.correctAnswer: Commands encapsulate both the operation and its reversal logic, making undo/redo trivial
blocks.explanation: The Command Pattern wraps an operation (Execute) and its inverse (Undo) in a single object. This means the history manager does not need to know what each command does — it just calls Execute() and Undo(). This enables features like undo/redo, action replay, macro recording, and branching history that would be impossible with direct state mutation.

parts.partTitle: Part 3: Observer Pattern, Reactive Programming & UniRx

blocks.value: Reactive Programming with UniRx
UniRx brings Reactive Extensions (Rx) to Unity, enabling declarative, composable event streams. Instead of polling or callback hell, you chain operators that react to data changes automatically.

items: IObservable<T> represents a stream of values over time
IObserver<T> subscribes to and reacts to those values
Operators like Where, Select, Throttle, Buffer, Merge compose streams
ReactiveProperty<T> is an observable variable that notifies on change
AsyncSubject, BehaviorSubject, ReplaySubject control stream behavior

blocks.output: ReactiveHealthSystem with ReactiveProperty, computed HealthPercent, throttled UI updates, death detection with Take(1), and combined input/health streams.

blocks.value: Advanced Stream Composition

blocks.output: Advanced stream composition: debounced auto-save, combo counting with Buffer, merged achievement conditions, FPS counter, and custom input observables.

blocks.question: What is the main benefit of using ReactiveProperty over a standard C# property with an event?
options: ReactiveProperty uses less memory
ReactiveProperty composes with LINQ-like operators (Where, Select, Throttle) and auto-manages subscriptions
ReactiveProperty is faster for single assignments
ReactiveProperty is built into Unity
blocks.correctAnswer: ReactiveProperty composes with LINQ-like operators (Where, Select, Throttle) and auto-manages subscriptions
blocks.explanation: A standard property with an event requires manual subscription management and imperative logic. ReactiveProperty is an IObservable that can be chained with operators like Where (filter), Throttle (rate limit), Buffer (window), and CombineLatest (merge streams). This enables declarative, composable reactive logic that is far more maintainable than callback spaghetti.

parts.partTitle: Part 4: ECS Deep Dive: Systems, Queries, Baking

blocks.value: Advanced ECS: System Scheduling & Queries
Production ECS requires understanding system scheduling, entity queries with change filtering, chunk iteration, and baking workflows for converting GameObjects to entities at build time.

blocks.output: Advanced ECS patterns: change filtering, EntityCommandBuffer for deferred operations, and direct chunk iteration for maximum performance.

blocks.value: Baking: Converting GameObjects to Entities

blocks.output: Baker converting MonoBehaviour to ECS components at build time, including shared components, dynamic buffers, entity references, and runtime instantiation of baked prefabs.

blocks.question: Why use an EntityCommandBuffer instead of directly modifying entities during system iteration?
options: EntityCommandBuffer is faster than direct modification
Entities cannot be created/destroyed during iteration; command buffers defer changes until after iteration completes
EntityCommandBuffer is required by the Burst compiler
EntityCommandBuffer automatically handles memory allocation
blocks.correctAnswer: Entities cannot be created/destroyed during iteration; command buffers defer changes until after iteration completes
blocks.explanation: During system iteration, the archetype chunks are locked for reading. Creating or destroying entities would invalidate chunk pointers and corrupt memory. EntityCommandBuffer records all structural changes and applies them atomically after the system completes. This is essential for safe multithreaded ECS code.

blocks.value: Unity Physics (DOTS) vs PhysX

Unity Physics is a DOTS-based physics engine that runs on the Job System with Burst compilation. Unlike PhysX (which is object-oriented and runs on the main thread), Unity Physics is data-oriented, multithreaded, and deterministic — critical for networked games and replay systems.

items: Deterministic: same inputs always produce same outputs across platforms
Multithreaded: broadphase and solver run on worker threads
Stateless: physics state is pure data, easy to serialize for rollback netcode
Custom colliders: Compound, Mesh, Convex, Capsule, Sphere, Box, Cylinder
No hidden state: everything is explicit IComponentData

blocks.output: Unity Physics system with custom gravity/drag, raycasting against the collision world, and collision event processing for damage application.

blocks.value: Deterministic Simulation & Replay

blocks.output: Deterministic simulation with state snapshots for rollback netcode, fixed timestep physics, and history trimming for memory management.

blocks.question: Why is Unity Physics (DOTS) preferable to PhysX for networked multiplayer games?
options: Unity Physics has better collision detection accuracy
Unity Physics is deterministic — same inputs produce same outputs, enabling rollback and replay
Unity Physics supports more collider shapes
Unity Physics is easier to configure in the Inspector
blocks.correctAnswer: Unity Physics is deterministic — same inputs produce same outputs, enabling rollback and replay
blocks.explanation: Determinism is critical for networked games. With deterministic physics, all clients can simulate the same world state from the same inputs without sending physics state over the network. This enables rollback netcode and replay systems. PhysX is not deterministic across platforms or even runs. Unity Physics achieves determinism through fixed-point math, consistent iteration order, and stateless design.

blocks.value: Scriptable Render Pipeline (SRP) Fundamentals

Unity's Scriptable Render Pipeline (SRP) lets you control every aspect of rendering. Unlike the Built-in RP (black box), SRP exposes the render loop as C# code you fully control. URP and HDRP are built on SRP — you can build your own.

items: RenderPipelineAsset configures the pipeline (settings, shaders, features)
ScriptableRenderContext is the bridge to the native rendering backend
CommandBuffers are replaced by RenderGraph for automatic resource management
Render Features inject custom passes into existing pipelines (URP/HDRP)
Profiling, GPU instancing, and draw call batching are fully exposed

blocks.output: Custom RenderPipelineAsset and RenderPipeline with culling, opaque/transparent drawing, skybox, dynamic batching, and GPU instancing control.

blocks.value: URP Render Feature: Custom Post-Processing Pass

blocks.output: URP Render Feature injecting a custom outline post-processing pass with material property control and proper resource cleanup.

blocks.question: What is the primary advantage of using a Render Feature over modifying URP's source code?
options: Render Features are faster than built-in passes
Render Features are modular, version-safe, and can be shared across projects without forking URP
Render Features support more shader types
Render Features are required for post-processing
blocks.correctAnswer: Render Features are modular, version-safe, and can be shared across projects without forking URP
blocks.explanation: Modifying URP source code creates maintenance nightmares when Unity updates. Render Features are self-contained ScriptableObjects that inject passes into the pipeline via the official API. They survive URP updates, can be packaged as reusable assets, and are toggled per-renderer without code changes.

blocks.value: Compute Shaders: Massively Parallel GPU Compute

Compute Shaders run general-purpose code on the GPU without being tied to the graphics pipeline. They are essential for GPU-driven rendering, particle systems, physics simulation, and procedural generation at scale.

blocks.output: GPU-driven particle system with compute shader spawn/update kernels, compute buffers, and DrawMeshInstancedIndirect for 100,000+ particles with zero CPU overhead.

blocks.value: GPU Frustum Culling & LOD Selection

blocks.output: GPU frustum culling with compute shader, LOD distance selection, and DrawMeshInstancedIndirect for culling 50,000 instances entirely on GPU.

blocks.question: What is the primary advantage of GPU-driven rendering (compute shaders + indirect draw) over CPU-driven rendering?
options: GPU-driven rendering uses simpler shaders
GPU-driven rendering eliminates CPU-GPU synchronization, allowing 100,000+ instances with near-zero CPU cost
GPU-driven rendering works on all platforms including mobile
GPU-driven rendering requires less VRAM
blocks.correctAnswer: GPU-driven rendering eliminates CPU-GPU synchronization, allowing 100,000+ instances with near-zero CPU cost
blocks.explanation: In CPU-driven rendering, the CPU must cull, sort, and issue draw calls for every object. GPU-driven rendering uploads instance data once, then the GPU handles culling (compute shader), LOD selection, and draw dispatch (indirect draw) without CPU involvement. This enables massive scene complexity (100,000+ objects) that would choke the CPU. The trade-off is higher GPU complexity and platform support requirements.

parts.partTitle: Part 8: Shader Graph Advanced: Custom Nodes, Subgraphs, LOD Crossfade

blocks.value: Custom Shader Graph Nodes via Code
Shader Graph's visual node system is powerful, but custom nodes unlock domain-specific logic that cannot be expressed with built-in nodes. You create them via C# and HLSL.

blocks.output: Custom Shader Graph nodes using CodeFunctionNode: World Space Curve with proper normal recalculation, and Simplex Noise 3D with configurable parameters.

blocks.value: LOD Crossfade & Dithering in Shader Graph

blocks.output: LOD crossfade controller with material property blocks, dither matrix for smooth LOD transitions, and coroutine-based transition timing.

blocks.question: Why create custom Shader Graph nodes instead of using Subgraphs?
options: Custom nodes are faster at runtime
Custom nodes can contain arbitrary HLSL logic that Subgraphs cannot express, and they are reusable across projects
Custom nodes work on mobile while Subgraphs do not
Custom nodes are easier to create than Subgraphs
blocks.correctAnswer: Custom nodes can contain arbitrary HLSL logic that Subgraphs cannot express, and they are reusable across projects
blocks.explanation: Subgraphs are visual groupings of existing nodes — they cannot contain custom HLSL. Custom nodes (CodeFunctionNode) let you write arbitrary shader code, implement complex algorithms (noise, curve deformation), and package them as reusable assets. They also expose proper inputs/outputs in the Shader Graph UI with type safety.

parts.partTitle: Part 9: HLSL Shader Programming: Vertex/Fragment/Geometry Shaders

blocks.value: Hand-Written HLSL Shaders

While Shader Graph covers 80% of needs, hand-written HLSL is required for: custom vertex displacement, geometry shaders for procedural mesh generation, tessellation for LOD terrain, and compute-like effects that Shader Graph cannot express.

blocks.output: Hand-written HLSL shader with Gerstner wave vertex displacement, normal recalculation, shadow mapping, and Fresnel water edge effect in URP.

blocks.value: Geometry Shader: Procedural Grass

blocks.output: Geometry shader generating procedural grass blades from triangle mesh, with wind animation, per-blade UVs, and gradient coloring from base to tip.

blocks.question: When should you use a geometry shader instead of vertex/fragment shaders?
options: Geometry shaders are always faster than vertex shaders
Geometry shaders are ideal for creating new geometry procedurally (grass, fur, particles) from existing mesh data
Geometry shaders work on mobile GPUs
Geometry shaders are required for shadow casting
blocks.correctAnswer: Geometry shaders are ideal for creating new geometry procedurally (grass, fur, particles) from existing mesh data
blocks.explanation: Geometry shaders execute between vertex and fragment stages, receiving a complete primitive (point, line, or triangle) and emitting zero or more new primitives. They are perfect for procedural effects like grass blades from terrain triangles, fur from mesh surfaces, or particle billboards from point data. However, they have significant performance cost and poor mobile support, so they should be used sparingly and only when vertex/fragment shaders cannot achieve the effect.

parts.partTitle: Part 10: Unity Netcode for GameObjects (NGO) & Multiplayer Architecture

blocks.value: NGO Architecture: Host, Client, Server

Unity Netcode for GameObjects (NGO) provides a high-level networking API built on top of transport layers. Understanding the architecture patterns (host-authoritative, dedicated server, relay) is critical for building robust multiplayer games.

blocks.output: NGO NetworkManager with player spawning, NetworkList for synchronized player data, ServerRpc for ready state, ClientRpc for game start, and proper connection/disconnection handling.

blocks.value: Networked Player Controller with Input Prediction

blocks.output: Networked player controller with client-side prediction, server reconciliation, anti-cheat speed validation, and smooth interpolation for remote players.

blocks.question: In a client-authoritative vs server-authoritative architecture, why is server-authoritative preferred for competitive multiplayer?
options: Server-authoritative uses less bandwidth
Server-authoritative prevents cheating by validating all game state changes on the server
Server-authoritative has lower latency
Server-authoritative is easier to implement
blocks.correctAnswer: Server-authoritative prevents cheating by validating all game state changes on the server
blocks.explanation: In client-authoritative models, clients report their own position, health, and actions. A hacked client can teleport, deal infinite damage, or see through walls. Server-authoritative architecture means the server simulates all physics, validates movement speeds, and only accepts legal state changes. Clients predict locally for responsiveness, but the server has final authority. This is the industry standard for competitive multiplayer.
